queue.title: Managing Key Clients: Revenue Concentration
queue.content:
Revenue driven largely by one client exposes a company to risk comparable to single-supplier dependence. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

A company whose revenue is largely driven by one client is actually exposed to a risk comparable to dependence on a single supplier.

A company whose revenue is largely driven by one client is actually exposed to a risk comparable to dependence on a single supplier.

When one client accounts for a significant share of total revenue, losing that relationship — whether from contract termination, a change of ownership, or a strategic client decision — can jeopardise the stability of the whole business.

Tracking the largest client's share of total revenue, with a defined threshold above which active diversification kicks in, turns concentration management into a measurable discipline.

Diversifying the client base doesn't have to mean turning down large deals; it means consciously tracking the ratio and actively seeking new relationships before dependence becomes critical.

Contract clauses extending the notice period before terminating a large contract give a company valuable time to adjust, instead of a sudden loss of revenue.

queue.title: Managing Service Level Agreements (SLAs)
queue.content:
An SLA never tested in practice offers false security until a real outage reveals the gap. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

An SLA never tested in practice offers a false sense of security until a real outage reveals the gap between promise and reality.

An SLA never tested in practice offers a false sense of security until a real outage reveals the gap between promise and reality.

A service level agreement promising 99.9% uptime sounds convincing, but rarely contains a clear definition of how that uptime is measured and who verifies the supplier's reports.

Penalties for SLA breaches are usually capped at that month's service fee, often disproportionately small compared to the actual business damage from a service outage.

Independent monitoring of critical service availability, rather than relying solely on the supplier's own reports, reveals the real state of affairs and strengthens negotiating position at contract renewal.

A business continuity plan that doesn't assume perfect supplier availability, but includes a concrete response to a supplier outage, is more effective than relying solely on contract terms.

queue.title: Data Center Capacity Planning
queue.content:
Underestimated future data-center capacity costs more to fix with emergency upgrades than timely planning. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

Underestimated future data-center capacity is more expensive to solve with emergency upgrades than with timely growth planning.

Underestimated future data-center capacity is more expensive to solve with emergency upgrades than with timely growth planning.

Demand for computing capacity is growing faster than the average infrastructure-planning cycle, especially in companies rapidly adopting AI and analytics tools.

An emergency capacity upgrade under pressure, once existing resources no longer meet demand, is almost always costlier and operationally riskier than a planned, gradual upgrade.

Regular capacity projections based on planned business growth, not just current state, allow negotiating better terms with infrastructure suppliers in advance.

Flexible models — a hybrid approach of owned and leased infrastructure — reduce the risk of miscalculating capacity in both directions, too little and too much.

Cjelovit tekst i izvor: https://gnk-asg.hr/en/publications/data-center-capacity-planning/
